cues.text: A Parish Retreat
On October 21, 2006, roughly 600 people gathered for Mass during a spiritual retreat at the parish of St. Martin of Tours in Tixtla, Mexico.
Father Leopoldo Roque and a visiting priest led the Mass, assisted by a religious sister distributing Communion.
As the sister carried a pyx of consecrated Hosts to a homebound parishioner, she noticed, with visible emotion, that one of the Hosts had begun to exude a reddish substance.
A Diocesan Commission
Bishop Alejo Zavala Castro of the Diocese of Chilpancingo-Chilapa convened a theological commission to examine the event.
In October 2009, he invited Dr. Ricardo Castanon Gomez to oversee formal scientific research into the Tixtla Host.
Gomez had previously led the scientific investigation of the Buenos Aires account.
Findings of Living Tissue
The research was conducted between 2009 and 2012 and presented at a 2013 international symposium in Chilpancingo.
It identified the tissue as myocardium, heart muscle, containing intact white blood cells, red blood cells, and active macrophages.
The researchers described this cellular activity as consistent with living rather than long-dead tissue, and comparable to findings from the Lanciano and Buenos Aires accounts.
A Diocesan Declaration, Not Yet a Papal One
On October 12, 2013, Bishop Zavala Castro formally recognized the supernatural character of the events at Tixtla, declaring the case a "Divine Sign."
His successor, Bishop Salvador Rangel Mendoza, later clarified in 2022 that this recognition remained a diocesan-level judgment, not a final determination.
The case has been forwarded to the Holy See, and formal papal approval, which alone would settle the matter definitively, has not yet been given.
Legacy
Tixtla stands, along with a small number of other twenty-first-century cases, as an example of the careful, multi-stage process the Church now applies to reported Eucharistic phenomena.

This process involves years of scientific study, a bishop's own diocesan judgment, and finally a decision reserved to Rome that, as of the diocese's own most recent public statements, remains pending.
The account is included here as a diocesan-recognized, Vatican-pending case rather than a formally and finally approved miracle.
